questions: During the episodes, does the child stop responding to their name or touch?
Do the episodes begin and end abruptly?
Do they last only a few seconds?
Do the eyelid fluttering episodes occur many times per day?
Are the episodes reliably triggered by bright light, sunlight, or closing the eyes?
Do the eyes roll upward during the eyelid fluttering?
Does the child have brief jerking movements of the arms, shoulders, or head?
Is there confusion, sleepiness, or a headache immediately afterward?
Does the child remain aware of the event afterward?
Have there been any episodes of whole-body stiffening or rhythmic shaking?
Have the episodes occurred shortly after waking?
Can the child suppress or voluntarily stop the eyelid fluttering?
Are similar episodes present in any close relatives?
Has the child’s development or school performance been affected?
Has the child ever had an abnormal electroencephalogram?
orders: Prolonged video-electroencephalography with awake and sleep recording, hyperventilation, photic stimulation, and repeated eye-closure testing
Brain MRI with an epilepsy protocol
Epilepsy-focused genetic testing if the EEG confirms generalized epilepsy or developmental impairment is significant
served: video-EEG monitoring of a typical event
results: 1. Prolonged video-electroencephalography with awake and sleep recording, hyperventilation, photic stimulation, and repeated eye-closure testing
video-EEG monitoring of a typical event: eyelid myoclonia with absences - the Jeavons phenotype
2. Brain MRI with an epilepsy protocol
brain MRI: punctate FLAIR hyperintensities in the local white matter of both frontal lobes
4. Epilepsy-focused genetic testing if the EEG confirms generalized epilepsy or developmental impairment is significant
genetic testing (exome / epilepsy panel): missense variant in exon 4 of CSNK2B (NM_001320.7 c.268A>C, p.Thr90Pro), likely pathogenic by ACMG; threonine 90 is evolutionarily conserved
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: CSNK2B-related Poirier–Bienvenu neurodevelopmental syndrome (POBINDS), caused by the heterozygous likely pathogenic CSNK2B p.Thr90Pro variant, presenting with eyelid myoclonia with absences (Jeavons phenotype)

1. Jeavons syndrome (genetic generalized epilepsy with eyelid myoclonia), independent of the CSNK2B variant
2. Another genetic generalized epilepsy syndrome with eyelid myoclonia and absences
3. CSNK2B-related epilepsy without sufficient neurodevelopmental impairment to establish POBINDS
order_raw:
1. Prolonged video-electroencephalography with awake and sleep recording, hyperventilation, photic stimulation, and repeated eye-closure testing
2. Brain MRI with an epilepsy protocol
3. Formal developmental and neuropsychological assessment
4. Epilepsy-focused genetic testing if the EEG confirms generalized epilepsy or developmental impairment is significant
